evidence: "The length of retrieved code snippets is set to half the prompt length." (Sec. 4 implementation details; prompt+output max 4,096 GPT-3.5 / 2,048 CodeGen)
note: Both arms are flat retrievers (Jaccard vs UniXcoder) over the same 20-line sliding windows, so not structure-vs-flat. Paper says the length is 'set to' half the prompt but never states fill/truncation or per-arm realized lengths; with K<=10 x 20-line snippets the half-prompt allocation is plausibly but not provably filled. No structured arm exists anywhere in the paper.

evidence: "We consider a maximum of 512 BPE tokens for such context, and the rest of the tokens will be truncated." (Sec. 3, retrieval setup; Table 4 retriever comparison)
note: Both arms flat (BM25 vs UniXCoder vs ada). Truncation is stated but top-5 x 10-line chunks may fall below 512 tokens, so fill is not guaranteed; per-arm realized tokens not reported. Differences are small (EM 15.72 / 15.87 / 16.47, StarCoder-15.5B Python).

structured_arm: In-file context + top-3 Tree-sitter AST-extracted 'abstract contexts' (declaration/signature skeletons) + Jaccard-ranked snippets, filled to N=4,096
flat_arm: In-file context + Jaccard-ranked 10-line snippet contexts only (abstracts removed from pool), filled to N=4,096
outcome: no clear difference: Table 2 R2C2-Bench average EM with vs without abstracts: StarCoder-7B 24.8 vs 24.3, DeepSeekCoder-6.7B 30.1 vs 29.5, Code Llama-7B 19.9 vs 19.7; average ES 49.2 vs 49.0, 54.8 vs 54.3, 41.6 vs 41.7.
evidence: "candidates are concatenated to the beginning of the in-file context based on their Jaccard similarity [28] in descending order, until the cumulative length, including the in-file context, reaches the maximum token limit of N=4096" (Sec. 4 'Retrieval with R2C2-Enhance')
note: Structured arm is hybrid (abstracts + snippets); abstracts are themselves selected by Jaccard similarity. Gains <=0.6 pp EM, ES even reverses for Code Llama; single run, no significance test. Realized per-arm lengths not reported. Table 5 ablation (31.2 vs 42.1) changes fine-tuning too and was not used.

evidence: "Prometheus with working memory achieves a resolution rate of 70.00% while incurring a total inference cost of $200.79 across 50 issues." (Sec. 4.3.1, Fig. 7; without memory $367.73)
note: Budget is dollars, not context tokens; 50 random SWE-bench Verified instances, single run. Varied factor is a working-memory cache, not structure: both arms use the same knowledge-graph context engine. The KG/AST representation is never ablated, so the paper has no structure-vs-flat test.

evidence: "Table 8: Token Usage per Question (Input/Output)." Rows: Function Chunking RAG 3,042 / 64; Sliding Window RAG 6,302/73 (App., Table 8)
note: Both arms retrieve top-10 chunks by voyage-code-3 embedding similarity; only chunk boundaries differ (parser-based function chunks vs 500-line windows). Judged chunking granularity, not structural context, hence false. If a reviewer counts function chunking as AST-structure, the outcome is flat better (Kimi K2 60.08 vs 62.44; GPT-5.1 66.57 vs 66.79; Qwen3-Coder-30B 63.40 vs 64.86) with the structured arm at ~half the input tokens. Token figures are identical across models (likely averaged).

evidence: "Compared with No_compression, SWEzze removes 13,150 prompt tokens per instance on DeepSeek-V3.2, 6,535 on Qwen3-Coder-Next, and 12,401 on GPT-5.2" (Sec. RQ1; Table 3: SWEzze 8658 vs LLMLingua-2 11,480)
note: Varied factor is the compression method (AST-segment cross-encoder pruner vs token-level LLMLingua-2); the model sees pruned raw code in both arms, so not structure-vs-flat. Nominal targets differ across baselines (defaults vs 5x); LongCodeZip and SWE-Pruner use fewer tokens than SWEzze on some models.

evidence: "Any unused tokens from this allocation are then filled by the cross-file context, up to a total prompt size of 6,400 tokens." (Sec. 5, RepoBench-P setup; Random: 'until the token limit is reached')
note: Both arms flat (UniXcoder ranking vs random). The candidate pool for both is snippets parsed from import statements, so import structure is held constant, not varied. Random arm run once (authors call results 'indicative and not conclusive'). Realized per-arm tokens not tabulated.

structured_arm: RC: rationale context only (signatures of imported modules/classes/methods derived from import analysis over the Code Knowledge Graph), RTG-ranked and truncated to L=256
flat_arm: AC: analogy context only (BM25-retrieved similar code chunks), RTG-ranked and truncated to L=256
outcome: flat better: DeepSeek-Coder-7B Code EM at L=256 (UniXcoder ranking) AC 15.87 vs RC 14.45; at L=512 AC > RC under all five rankers (e.g. UniXcoder 18.72 vs 17.71, Jaccard 18.39 vs 16.47). At L=256 RC edges AC only with CodeBERT (13.02 vs 12.91) and Random (12.8 vs 12.46) ranking.
evidence: "(Truncation constraint) The total length of all the items in \Gamma_{td} is bounded by the length bound L" (Sec. 3.3, Def. Truncated Dual Context; Appendix A table)
note: Switched from the checker's DC-vs-AC pick: RC-vs-AC is the cleaner structure-vs-flat test. As a complement, the dependency context helps: DC (AC+RC) beats AC at L=256 (17.15 vs 15.87 EM). Realized tokens not reported; only mean item counts (~1 item per arm at 256), and RTG keeps whole items, so arms may not reach L. Appendix results cover one model only; at L=4096 the cap is not binding ('approximate it as Unlimited').

structured_arm: Imports First composer: repository files ordered by first-degree import relation to the completion file, truncated to the cap
flat_arm: Naive composer: all repository files concatenated in no specific order, truncated to the same cap
outcome: structure better (perplexity, lower is better): All files 1.791 vs 1.798 @256, 1.769 vs 1.788 @1,753, 1.732 vs 1.761 @12,000; Python-only 1.785 vs 1.788, 1.751 vs 1.760, 1.666 vs 1.677 (Table 10).
evidence: "A number in the column name means the maximum number of tokens in the context from the repository snapshot." (App. C, Table 10)
note: Switched from Path distance vs Naive (file-tree proximity is not program structure) to Imports First vs Naive. The metric is perplexity on the completion file, CodeLlama-7B only, single run, and the differences are small. Fill is inferred from the composers concatenating 48K-192K-char repositories; the paper does not state it. Counter-evidence: the declarations-only skeleton (+PD) is worse than PD with full files at the same cap (1.710 vs 1.607 @12k).

evidence: "The retrieved chunks are then added to C_retr in descending order of relevance until the input length reaches the predefined length L ." (Sec. 3 RAG; L=10,240; Table 5 on samples >10k tokens)
note: Both arms flat (two embedding models). With 4,096-token chunks, the fill is coarse-grained. Realized tokens not reported. Single model (fine-tuned DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B).

structured_arm: GraphCoder: snippets retrieved via code-context-graph (control-flow/data-dependence) slices, within the 2,048-token window
flat_arm: RLCoder: learned similarity-based retriever of cross-file snippets, within the same 2,048-token window
outcome: flat better: GPT-5, preceding context, EM/ES GraphCoder vs RLCoder: Chisel 11.1/17.3 vs 17.9/55.3; V/SV 14.3/35.4 vs 23.8/55.9; VHDL 7.8/33.1 vs 26.6/61.4; HLS 16.2/25.2 vs 17.4/56.2 (Table 4). GraphCoder is also below No RAG (Chisel 15.2/51.6).
evidence: "All models use a fixed 2,048-token input window." (Sec. 4 'Retrieval Framework and Prompt'); No-RAG prompts: "the head of the left context and the tail of the right context are trimmed" (Figs. 7-8)
note: Switched to GraphCoder vs RLCoder: both single-call retrieval at the same window, which is cleaner than vs No RAG. RepoCoder is iterative and adds calls. GraphCoder was ported to HDL by the benchmark authors (tree-sitter-cpp for HLS; it filters definition nodes), so this is partly an implementation/domain failure (App. A.6). Truncation is described only for No-RAG prompts; realized tokens not reported. GraphCoder snippets have half the mean length of RepoCoder's (Table 9).

structured_arm: TREEFRAG LOD-1: hierarchical repository tree of node names only (LLM-assisted decomposition of code/GUI/DB), plus the Ask (8k-12k tokens)
flat_arm: Naive: raw code base plus the Ask (194k-239k tokens)
outcome: no clear difference on mean score: 91.95 vs 91.24 (SD 4.48 vs 6.70, Table 8); per-Ask ranks favour TREEFRAG: mean rank 20.69 vs 24.69, first place 22/40 vs 5/40 (Table 9).
evidence: "TREEFRAG method: In this method, only the RWT hierarchical tree is sent at LOD 1 (node names only) along with the user's Ask. Token counts are between 8k and 12k." (Sec. 8.2)
note: Switched from TREEFRAG vs Function Summary (LLM summaries are neither flat nor program structure) to TREEFRAG vs Naive. Token counts are given as ranges across models, not per instance. The budget is uncontrolled (~20x smaller). The tree is built by LLM summarization rather than a parser. One application (RWT); LLM-as-grader; Naive excludes Claude models, so the rank pools differ. Industry paper (patents pending).

evidence: "SWE-Pruner Pro is the only pruner that reduces tokens on every cell, with savings up to 39% on the heaviest cell (Qwen3-Coder-Next, SWE-QA-Pro)" (Sec. 5, Table 1: 368K vs SWE-Pruner 433K vs No Pruning 607K)
note: Varied factor is the pruning model of tool outputs (raw window), not structure. Tokens are total agent tokens (an outcome, not a cap). Score differences are small (7.84 vs 7.36 vs 7.60).

structured_arm: SC-classExprTypes: 20% of the 1,536-token prompt budget filled with the files defining the types of all expressions in the class (static type analysis), rest local file, left-truncated
flat_arm: SC Standard: local file content up to the dereference point, left-truncated to the 1,536-token budget
outcome: structure better: SantaCoder score@6, classExprTypes vs Standard (both without MGD): CR 64.57 vs 59.97, NIM 84.91 vs 82.40, ISM 39.67 vs 38.14, PM 33.55 vs 32.10 (Table 1).
evidence: "We fix a prompt budget of (2048-512)=1536 tokens, and generation budget of 512 tokens, for a total context window size of 2048. If the text exceeds the prompt budget, we truncate it from the left" (App. D)
note: Switched from the checker's SC vs SC-MGD comparison: MGD injects structure through logit masking (a decoding constraint), so that pair is not structure-vs-flat. It was cap-matched only through identical prompts. classExprTypes vs Standard is an in-prompt structure-vs-flat contrast under the same cap. Fill holds only when the local file exceeds the budget; realized tokens not reported. Java, SantaCoder-1.1B, 6 samples per item.

evidence: Table II rows: "RAG (Sliding Window) | 58.48 | 31.60 | 4.2x" and "LongCodeZip | 60.58 | 35.40 | 5.3x"; Ratio = |C_original| / |C_compressed| (Eq. 7)
note: Realized compression ratio is reported per arm (averaged), and the proposed arm compresses more. The varied factor is the compression method (perplexity-ranked function chunks + knapsack vs similarity retrieval); not structure-vs-flat. RAG-Function-Chunking compresses harder (5.7x) at 57.93/30.80. 10 repeats with Wilcoxon test.

Both arms use repository-call-graph-derived usage patterns; only the call-graph-based clustering step is toggled, so not structure-vs-flat. Note the input record's arm_a/arm_b labels are swapped. '# Token' is likely the whole-pipeline average, not prompt context alone. Single run on DevEval with GPT-4o-mini; difference is 0.43 pp. Removing patterns entirely halves tokens (1407), so that ablation is not matched.

structured_arm: RepoMap: vectorless file ranking from path, symbol, reference and repository-graph signals, packed into 8k tokens
flat_arm: Qwen3-8B embedding (or BM25) file ranking, packed into the same 8k tokens
outcome: no clear difference vs the strongest flat retriever: BCY@8k weighted RepoMap 0.3788 vs Qwen3-8B 0.3732 (macro 0.3717 vs 0.3892 favours Qwen3-8B); structure better vs BM25 (0.3788 vs 0.2051) (Table 4).
evidence: "greedily packs files by rank, and prefix-truncates only at the budget boundary. ... Path headers and separator newlines count against the budget." (Sec. 4 metrics, BCY definition)
note: Retrieval-only metric (gold-file exposure in a packed budget), no generating LLM. The budget uses a regex tokenizer, not an LLM tokenizer. RepoMap mixes lexical path/symbol signals with graph signals. 16k/32k points may be lower bounds; 8k is filled because the median gold file has 515 lines.

evidence: "%RAG = ratio of instances where RAG is performed." (Table 3 caption); cross-file context "right-truncate[d] ... to 512 tokens" (App. A)
note: The selective arm omits cross-file context on 22-39% of instances, so the arms do not share a filled cap. Per-arm realized tokens are not reported; %RAG is only a proxy. The selective arm is smaller by construction, so this is a borderline structured-smaller, but tokens are never measured. No structured arm in the paper (Jaccard retrieval only).

structured_arm: HCP: current file + import-dependency (D1) files with global context removed + other files as function-level skeletons/embedding-sampled functions (top-k=5)
flat_arm: Random-All: all repository files randomly concatenated, left-truncated to the model window (16,352 / 8,160)
outcome: structure better: Table 4 (top-k=5) vs Random-All: StarCoder2-7B EM 35.76 vs 31.45, ES 71.41 vs 69.09; DScoder-6.7B EM 39.74 vs 33.94, ES 73.90 vs 70.98.
evidence: "In our experiments, the HCP successfully reduced the input from over 50,000 tokens to approximately 8,000 tokens" (Sec. 1); "All the prompts longer than the model_max_length are truncated from the left." (Sec. 4)
note: Realized HCP lengths are only plotted (Fig. 4 right, by top-p at top-k=5); the text gives just '~8,000'. Table 4 uses top-p 1.0, whose length is not stated in the text. For CodeGemma (8,160 window) the arms are roughly equal in size. HCP is hybrid (embedding-sampled functions). Top-k 0 row (no sampled functions) also beats Random-All (StarCoder2-7B EM 32.62 vs 31.45). Single run.

evidence: Table 5: GPT-5.2 Lite "Search returns full code content | 69.3% | 218k" vs "Search returns code preview + specialized filtering | 70.8% | 197k"
note: Both arms navigate the same dependency-derived code-structure tree. The varied factor is skeleton previews + two-stage filtering vs full code in search returns, i.e. content granularity within a structured pipeline, so judged not structure-vs-flat (borderline). Tokens are total input+output agent tokens (an outcome); gains are 0.6-1.5 pp.

evidence: Table 3, LongCodeQA 4x: "SWE-Pruner | ... | 13.95 | 59.46" vs "LaMR | ... | 16.48 | 61.26" (1/\tau = realized compression)
note: Varied factor is the pruner (rubric CRFs + AST-aware repair vs single CRF); both arms feed pruned raw code, so not structure-vs-flat. On LCC, LaMR keeps more tokens (4.37x vs 5.56x at 4x; 9.17x vs 10.92x at 8x), so the smaller-arm claim holds only for LongCodeQA. AST-repair ablation (Table 8, 18.51x vs 18.00x at 8x) is also pruning-internal. Single run.

structured_arm: Mini-SWE-Agent bash interface + SeeRepo graph tool returning rendered images of the AST-derived contains/imports/invokes/inherits dependency graph
flat_arm: Same agent with the standard bash text interface only
outcome: no clear difference: Pass@1 GPT-5-mini 55.4% vs 55.0% (input tokens 144,403 vs 193,157); GPT-5.1 48.8% vs 51.0%; Kimi K2.5 70.6% vs 68.8% (tokens +5%); Doubao +1.0 (Table 2).
evidence: "On GPT-5-mini, Pass@1 improves to 55.4% (+0.4) with input tokens reduced by 25% and cost by 26%." (Sec. 1 findings; Table 2)
note: Tokens are an outcome under shared $3/250-step limits, not a controlled budget. The structured arm is smaller for GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.1 and Doubao and ~5% larger for Kimi. The structured arm keeps bash too (additive tool). The graph arrives as images, so token accounting depends on image-token pricing. Single Pass@1 run; direction mixed across models.

evidence: "Paritok-4B compresses agent context to 25.7% of its size, versus 50.2% for the gpt-4.1-mini compressor and 61.9% for gpt-5" (Sec. 6.2, Table 9)
note: Varied factor is the compressor model (extractive 4B LoRA vs prompted gpt-4.1-mini); both feed compressed raw oracle context, so not structure-vs-flat. Single-shot harness on SWE-bench Lite; the authors state the 0.9-point quality gap is not separable.

structured_arm: GraphCoder: statement-level snippets retrieved by coarse-to-fine matching over code context graph (control-flow + control/data-dependence) slices, half the window, <=10 snippets
flat_arm: Vanilla RAG: 20-line sliding windows retrieved by Jaccard similarity of the preceding context, same half-window and <=10 snippets
outcome: structure better: Code EM GraphCoder vs Vanilla RAG, Python: CodeGen2-16B API-level 48.75 vs 35.80, line-level 46.65 vs 39.00; StarCoder-15B API 38.90 vs 35.90, line 34.50 vs 32.80; GPT-3.5 API 45.25 vs 37.50, line 46.60 vs 37.90 (Table 2).
evidence: "the difference in the number of tokens is not significant, as we employ the same prompt template and organization method for retrieved results in the prompt." (Sec. 6.4.3; Table 5 #In: 3715.51 vs 3882.12, 2201.08 vs 2239.95, 2666.13 vs 2557.12)
note: Input tokens are within ~4.3% for all three models (GraphCoder smaller for StarCoder/CodeGen2, 4.3% larger for GPT-3.5). Token counts are averaged over all tasks, not per subset. Temperature 0, single run, no significance test. Authors' own benchmark (RepoEval-derived).

structured_arm: RepoScope: four-view context (callers, call-graph-predicted call chains, similar functions, similar fragments) with structure-preserving serialization, ~4096-token allocation
flat_arm: SimpleRAG: fixed set of similarity-retrieved code snippets appended to the prompt, one-shot
outcome: structure better: Pass@1 CoderEval RepoScope vs SimpleRAG: GPT-4o mini 44.93 vs 39.13, Claude-3.5-Haiku 55.07 vs 43.96, Qwen3-235B 49.28 vs 43.00, DeepSeek-V3 59.42 vs 48.79; DevEval 26.18 vs 22.61, 41.56 vs 28.42, 30.02 vs 21.81, 35.82 vs 28.53 (Table 2).
evidence: "we adjusted parameters in baselines during evaluation to make sure their average prompt token lengths were approximately at the same level." (Sec. 5; Table 2 Avg. # Token: RepoScope 3679 vs SimpleRAG 3824 CoderEval, 3803 DevEval)
note: Switched from w/o SS, where both arms carry the same call-chain entities and only the serialization differs (both structured), to RepoScope vs SimpleRAG. Token gap is 3.3-3.8%. RepoScope is hybrid and multi-component (it includes similarity views), so this is not a single-factor ablation. RepoScope's average 3679 is identical on both datasets, which is worth checking. RLCoder uses fewer tokens (3576/3668) and scores lower.
Budget is per-instance USD cost (an outcome), not tokens. Varied factor is trajectory-history management (masking old observations); no structure. Direction varies across models (-11.8% to +8.5%).

evidence: "All baseline methods are configured to match identical compression constraints (4x and 8x) under the same experimental conditions." (App.); realized 1/\tau in Table 4: 10.92 vs RAG 6.60 (LCC 8x)
note: Same nominal target, but realized compression differs, with SWE-Pruner keeping fewer tokens than every baseline. Varied factor is the pruning method (line-level reranker vs token pruning / function-chunk RAG), not structure-vs-flat. Single model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct).

structured_arm: Mini-SWE-agent + Caller-Centric Exploration toolkit (dependency-graph tools: caller patterns, call hierarchy, graph queries)
outcome: structure better: GPT-5 Mini on ReCUBE-large APR 57.72 vs 54.47 (+3.25 pp, Table 6) at $0.1166 vs $0.1410 per instance and 19.81 vs 25.66 turns (Table 7).
evidence: Table 7 (GPT-5-mini, Large): "Agent | $ 0.1410 | 25.66 | 221.4" vs "Agent (Ours) | $ 0.1166 | 19.81"
note: Cost in USD and reported for GPT-5 Mini only; other models have no cost data. On original ReCUBE, CCE costs 1.2% more ($0.1241 vs $0.1226), which is near-equal, with SPR ~38.78 vs ~31.22 (derived from SPR/Cost). The CCE arm adds tools on top of bash. Single run; cost is an outcome, not a control.

evidence: Table 4: "Total tokens (thousands) | 23/30 | 222.79 | 179.31 | -43.48 | [-82.01,-13.80]" (Q6 provider substitution)
note: Both providers are graph-backed (CodeNib SCIP symbol-graph views vs LocAgent's code graph), so not structure-vs-flat. Tokens cover only 23/30 tasks; recall CI spans zero (+8.70 [-12.41,+29.50]). The graph-vs-dense test (Q1 graph expansion) holds the same candidate count but is retrieval-only with no LLM and no token budget, and every interval includes zero.
